chunks.topic: Knee pain, stiffness and numbness in weeks 4-6
chunks.content: Four to six weeks after a knee replacement, pain is usually less intense than in the first days, but aching after exercise, stiffness and some swelling are still common. Most people feel some stiffness, particularly when they bend the knee a long way, and it is often noticeable after sitting for a while. Keeping up the prescribed bending, straightening and strengthening exercises is the main way to reduce stiffness. Rehabilitation guidelines advise that if the range of motion stops improving and the end of the bend feels hard or painful, the physiotherapist should contact the surgeon, so mention this early rather than waiting.

chunks.topic: Knee pain in the first week after knee replacement
chunks.content: It helps to plan exercise sessions for times when your pain relief is working well and to rest with the leg supported in between. If the knee aches or swells after activity, raise the leg and cool it with an ice pack wrapped in a towel. Pain when bending the knee in this first week is expected, but overall it should be slowly settling rather than steadily getting worse. Contact your surgical team promptly if pain keeps increasing both at rest and with movement, if it is not controlled by the pain relief you were given, or if it comes with fever, shaking chills, increasing redness or drainage at the wound, or new pain and swelling in the calf. Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain needs emergency help straight away, because it can mean a blood clot has reached the lungs.

chunks.topic: Is my knee recovery on track? What steady progress looks like
chunks.content: Useful markers from the HSS guideline are about 80 degrees of bending by the end of the first week, more than 110 degrees with a fully straight knee by around six weeks, and more than 120 degrees for people aiming to return to demanding activities, but your own team's targets take priority. A knee that is still swollen and stiff at four to six weeks is common and does not by itself mean recovery is slow, because mild to moderate swelling can last three to six months. Talk to your physiotherapist or surgeon if your range of motion stops improving or the end of the bend feels hard and painful, if you cannot straighten the knee fully, if pain is increasing rather than decreasing, or if you cannot progress your walking.

chunks.topic: Knee pain in the first week after knee replacement
chunks.content: Pain is expected after a total knee replacement and is a normal part of healing. In the first days the knee is usually sore, swollen and stiff, and it commonly hurts more when you bend it, walk, or do your exercises. Care teams usually combine more than one kind of pain relief so you can move comfortably; take whatever you have been prescribed exactly as directed, and ask the team before changing anything. Movement is part of pain control rather than something to avoid. A physical therapist normally starts knee exercises within hours of the operation, and although the exercises can feel uncomfortable at first, doing them regularly speeds recovery and actually lowers pain over the following days.

chunks.topic: Knee pain at night after knee replacement
chunks.content: Many people find that the knee aches more in the evening and at night, and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that it is common for the knee to hurt at night and with activity for several weeks after surgery. By the end of the day the knee can feel sore and swollen from walking and exercise, so a few habits can make nights easier. Spread your walks and exercise sessions through the day instead of doing everything at once. In the evening, rest with the leg raised and use ice for a while to settle swelling. When lying down, keep the knee straight: do not sleep with a pillow under the knee, because a knee that rests bent for long periods can lose its ability to fully straighten.

chunks.topic: Knee pain at night after knee replacement
chunks.content: NHS guidance says no particular sleeping position is required after a knee replacement, so choose whatever is comfortable while keeping the knee straight; propping the heel on a small rolled towel, as in your straightening exercise, is one way to support the leg. If night pain is regularly stopping you from sleeping, tell your surgical team or physiotherapist. They may suggest changing when you take your prescribed pain relief or adjusting your activity plan, but do not change your medicines on your own. Night pain should slowly become less of a problem over the weeks. Pain that is steadily getting worse instead of easing, pain at rest together with fever or redness around the wound, or new calf pain and swelling should be checked promptly rather than waiting for your next appointment.

chunks.topic: What to expect two to three weeks after knee replacement
chunks.content: Swelling, stiffness, and some pain with activity and at night are still common at this stage, and some days will feel worse than others. You may still need help with some household tasks. Keep wearing compression stockings if advised, raise the leg when resting, avoid standing still for long periods, and avoid twisting the knee, bending down and reaching up where you can. Hold off kneeling on the new knee until your doctor approves it, and avoid crossing your legs when sitting for the first six weeks. Keep the wound clean and dry and follow your team's advice about showering. Contact your team if the wound becomes red, hot or starts to drain, if you have a fever, or if calf pain or new swelling develops.

chunks.topic: Early exercises in the first week after knee replacement
chunks.content: Exercise usually starts very soon after a knee replacement, often within hours, and a physical therapist will teach you a home programme before you leave hospital. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes a set of early exercises that most programmes include. Quadriceps sets: tighten the front thigh muscle and try to straighten the knee, holding for five to ten seconds. Straight leg raises: with the thigh tightened and the knee fully straight, lift the leg a few inches off the bed, hold briefly and lower it slowly. Ankle pumps: move the foot up and down rhythmically for a couple of minutes, several times an hour, to keep the blood moving.

chunks.topic: Returning to exercise and sport after knee replacement
chunks.content: The Hospital for Special Surgery guideline advises avoiding high-impact activities such as running, jumping and plyometric exercise in weeks seven to twelve, while strength, balance and endurance are rebuilt with leg presses, step-ups and step-downs, squats against a wall or ball, and treadmill, elliptical or bicycle work. It notes that expert opinion varies widely on which sports are advisable after a knee replacement, so return to a particular sport should be agreed with your surgeon, and sport-specific training, if appropriate, usually comes later and only with the surgeon's clearance. Signs that you are progressing well include little increase in pain or swelling after activity, climbing stairs foot over foot, and managing tasks such as putting on socks and tying shoelaces yourself.

chunks.topic: Returning to exercise and sport after knee replacement
chunks.content: Two to three months after a knee replacement, many people are ready to do more, and eventually most can return to many of the sports they enjoyed before surgery. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons stresses not doing too much, too soon, and continuing the exercises your physical therapist prescribed for at least two months after surgery. Walk as much as you like, but remember that walking does not replace your prescribed exercises. Swimming is an excellent low-impact activity once the wound has fully healed and your doctor agrees. In general, lower-impact activities such as golf, cycling and pickleball are easier on the knee and are generally a better choice than high-impact activities such as jogging, jumping and skiing.

chunks.topic: Early exercises in the first week after knee replacement
chunks.content: Knee straightening: place a small rolled towel just above the heel, tighten the thigh and try to press the back of the knee down towards the bed. Bed-supported knee bends: slide the heel towards the buttock to bend the knee, hold, and then straighten. Sitting knee bends: sit in a chair and bend the knee back as far as you can, using the other leg for support if needed. Repeat each exercise until the muscles feel tired, and follow the number of repetitions and sessions your own physiotherapist sets, because programmes differ. The Hospital for Special Surgery guideline gives the first-week aims as switching the thigh muscle back on, getting the knee as straight as possible, starting to regain bend, controlling swelling and walking safely with an aid.

chunks.topic: Walking aids, moving off the walker, and stairs after hip replacement
chunks.content: There is no fixed date for giving up the walking aid, because it depends on strength, balance and how steadily you walk, and your physical therapist will help you decide which aids you need and when they can safely be stopped. For stairs, remember 'up with the good, down with the bad': lead with the non-operated leg going up and with the operated leg coming down, one step at a time at first. Always use a handrail, do not attempt steps higher than standard height, and consider asking someone to stay close by on the stairs until your strength has largely returned. As you become stronger you can begin climbing stairs foot over foot. Check with your physiotherapist before you stop using your aid, especially if you feel unsteady or still need it because of pain.

chunks.topic: Walking aids, moving off the walker, and stairs after hip replacement
chunks.content: Walking is central to recovery after a hip replacement, and you will need a walking frame or crutches at first. Move the frame or crutches forward a short distance, then step forward with the operated leg, knee straight, so the heel touches the floor first, and bring the other leg through. NHS guidance is to walk every day as far as is comfortable and to tell your physiotherapist about any problems. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons suggests changing to one crutch or a cane once you are able to stand and walk for over ten minutes and the leg is strong enough that you no longer rely on the frame or crutches to take its weight; hold the cane in the hand opposite the operated hip.

chunks.topic: What you may be able to do two to three weeks after hip replacement
chunks.content: Your exercise programme will usually include bed exercises and standing exercises such as knee raises, hip abduction and hip extension several times a day. You should be able to get in and out of bed using the technique you were taught and manage stairs one step at a time with a handrail. At this stage you are still following your hip precautions, which usually last for about the first six weeks, such as not bending the hip beyond a right angle, not crossing your legs and avoiding low chairs. Some discomfort with activity and at night, and swelling in the leg and foot, are still common. It is too early to drive: NHS guidance is to wait at least six weeks. Most people resume light everyday activities within three to six weeks, so there is still steady progress to come.

chunks.topic: Recovery around four to six weeks after hip replacement
chunks.content: Around four to six weeks after a hip replacement, many people are noticeably more independent. Walking distance is usually increasing, and your physical therapist will advise when you can safely reduce or stop using your walking aid. Exercise programmes often add an exercise bike and resistance work around this time, with bike tension increased gradually from about four to six weeks. Hip precautions commonly apply for about the first six weeks, and most patients can do most of the restricted movements after six to eight weeks, but wait for your surgeon to confirm that yours have ended.

chunks.content: The speed of recovery after a hip replacement varies from person to person, depending on factors such as age and general health, so a slower pace than a friend or relative is not necessarily a problem. chunks.topic: Leg and foot swelling and discomfort after hip replacement
chunks.content: Swelling and discomfort in the operated leg are common after a hip replacement. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons warns that swelling is often moderate to severe during the first weeks, and the thigh, ankle and foot can all look puffy. NHS guidance notes that pain and swelling in the legs and feet usually improve over a few weeks, while the AAOS adds that milder swelling can continue for three to six months. To reduce swelling, raise the leg slightly when resting, apply ice for short periods, and wear compression stockings if they have been recommended. Try not to sit still for long periods: NHS guidance is to sit in a reclining position but get up and move regularly, because long spells without moving make swelling worse.
